posts.character: Childhood rules and rituals (bobbing for apples)
posts.quote: BOBBING FOR APPLES MEANT A WET FACE, A SOAKED COLLAR, AND ONE APPLE YOU REALLY EARNED.
posts.caption: Every fall party had a galvanized washtub sitting on the back porch, filled to the brim with cold water and a dozen apples bobbing around like they were laughing at you. Hands behind your back, no exceptions. You'd chase one around the edge of the tub with your teeth until your nose went under and you came up sputtering. The big kids knew the trick was to pin it against the bottom. The little kids just got wet. Somebody's mother always stood by with a dish towel, and nobody went home dry.
posts.first:
My cousin Ronnie figured out you could get the stem in your teeth and he won every year until we caught on. I never got one on the first try in my life. I still remember how cold that water was in October.

posts.quote: A METAL LUNCHBOX, A THERMOS THAT ALWAYS LEAKED, AND A BOLOGNA SANDWICH YOU'D TRADE FOR ANYTHING.
posts.caption: You carried it by that little handle, and it banged against your leg the whole way to school. Inside was the same lunch most days: a bologna sandwich in wax paper, an apple, and maybe two cookies if Mom was feeling generous. The thermos held milk or soup and leaked a little no matter how tight you screwed the lid. By lunchtime the sandwich tasted faintly of whatever was in that thermos. Nobody minded. The real business happened at the lunch table, where a bologna sandwich could be traded for a peanut butter and jelly if you knew how to deal.
posts.first:
Mine was plaid, red and green, and it had a dent in the lid from the time I used it as a step stool. The thermos glass broke twice and Dad replaced the insert both times instead of buying a new one. That lunchbox lasted me through fifth grade.

posts.quote: THE CHURCH SUPPER HAD SIX KINDS OF CASSEROLE AND NOT ONE WRITTEN RECIPE.
posts.caption: Once every fall the church basement filled up with long folding tables, paper tablecloths, and the best cooking in the county. Every woman in the congregation brought her specialty, and every one of them knew exactly whose dish was whose without looking at the name on the tape. Green bean, tuna noodle, scalloped potatoes, something with crushed potato chips on top. Nobody wrote anything down. If you asked for the recipe, you got a list of handfuls and pinches and a look that said you'd never get it right anyway. The men set up the chairs, the kids ran laps around the coat rack, and somebody always had to be sent home for more coffee.
posts.first:
Mrs. Lindquist made a hotdish with tater tots on top that people lined up for before the prayer was finished. My mother asked her for the recipe three different years. She never once gave the same answer twice.

posts.quote: THE ELEVATOR OPERATOR / WHITE GLOVES, A BRASS LEVER, AND EVERY FLOOR CALLED OUT BY HEART
posts.caption: In the big department store downtown, you didn't push a button. You stepped into a little wood-paneled room and told the lady in the uniform where you were headed. She'd slide the brass gate shut, work the lever, and stop that car level with the floor every single time without looking. Then she'd call it out like a train conductor: third floor, ladies' coats, hats, and gloves. She knew where every department was and which floor had the restrooms. Riding up with her felt like part of the trip, and the kids always wanted to stand right next to her to watch her work.
posts.first:
Mom took us downtown every year before Christmas, and the best part for me wasn't the toys. It was the elevator lady with her white gloves calling out the floors. I practiced saying it in her voice for weeks afterward.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (phone book booster seat)
posts.quote: NOBODY OWNED A BOOSTER SEAT. THAT'S WHAT THE PHONE BOOK WAS FOR.
posts.caption: When you were too short to reach the table, nobody went out and bought special equipment. Mom just pulled the phone book off the shelf by the kitchen phone and set it on your chair. If you were really little, the big Christmas catalog went on top of it. You sat up there like a king, swinging your feet, and the whole stack slid a little every time you reached for the potatoes. When the new phone book came in the mail, the old one got promoted to the dining room for good. It held you up through supper and was back by the phone in time for somebody to look up a number.
posts.first:
At Grandma's house it was two phone books and a throw pillow for me, and my little sister got the same stack plus the big family Bible on top. Grandpa said it was the only time that Bible ever held anybody up at the supper table.
